title: Membranes and transport
note: The plasma membrane is a fluid phospholipid bilayer studded with proteins. Small nonpolar molecules slip through; ions and polar molecules need protein channels or carriers. Passive transport runs down a gradient with no ATP; active transport pushes substances against a gradient and costs energy.

read.title: Getting across the membrane
text: The plasma membrane is mostly a double layer of phospholipids, with hydrophilic heads facing the watery fluids on each side and hydrophobic tails tucked inside. That oily core decides what can pass. Small nonpolar molecules such as oxygen and carbon dioxide dissolve in it and diffuse straight through. Ions and large polar molecules such as glucose cannot.

For those, cells use proteins. Channel proteins form water-filled pores; aquaporins, for example, let water stream across. Carrier proteins bind a solute and change shape to release it on the other side. When substances move this way from high to low concentration, the process is facilitated diffusion, and it needs no ATP.

Water itself moves by osmosis toward the side with more dissolved solute. A red blood cell in pure water swells and can burst, while one in very salty water shrivels. A plant cell in pure water simply becomes firm, because its wall pushes back.

Sometimes a cell must move a substance uphill, against its gradient. That is active transport, and it costs energy. The sodium-potassium pump spends one ATP to move three sodium ions out and two potassium ions in. The gradients it builds then power other transporters.
